title: Sympathetic Activation
subtitle: Mobilising heart, lungs, muscles and attention
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating sympathetic activation across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain sympathetic activation in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in sympathetic activation.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to sympathetic activation.

sections.explainSimply: Sympathetic activation increases readiness for action during perceived threat.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Tachycardia, sweating, tremor and vigilance may be misread as danger, reinforcing panic, avoidance or trauma cues.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Brainstem and hypothalamic pathways coordinate noradrenergic and autonomic output; interoceptive prediction influences how sensations are interpreted.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of sympathetic activation as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need sympathetic activation to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: High arousal is not always fear, and low arousal is not always safety.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use sympathetic activation to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses sympathetic activation to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: High arousal is not always fear, and low arousal is not always safety. Evidence classification: established physiology.
